name: Friction loss
seoTitle: Friction loss Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Friction loss: work out pipe length from the pipe diameter and the volumetric flow rate. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: The Friction loss calculator turns the pipe diameter, the volumetric flow rate and the friction head loss into pipe length. That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Friction loss calculator work?
sections.html:
The Friction loss calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports pipe length in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the material); then you type in the pipe diameter, the volumetric flow rate and the friction head loss.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in cubic meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 40 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 49 options, such as acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS), aluminium and asbestos Cement. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Friction loss calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Pipe length=(100 ÷ 1067) × friction head loss ÷ ((volumetric flow rate ÷ pipe roughness coefficient ^ 463 ÷ 250) ÷ (pipe diameter ^ 3044 ÷ 625))
Pressure loss=9810 × friction head loss

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in meters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Shown in bars, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Pressure, opening in bars

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Friction loss calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the pipe diameter, the volumetric flow rate and the friction head loss — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Friction loss calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns pipe length, derived from the pipe diameter, the volumetric flow rate and the friction head loss. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Friction loss calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the pipe diameter, the volumetric flow rate and the friction head loss, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter pipe diameter in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Pipe diameter opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Pipe roughness coefficient = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Friction loss calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
